title: The Church Leader Who Loved Attention
paragraphs:
The Church Leader Who Loved Attention
The applause felt holy... until it became his idol.
There is a scandal that rarely makes headlines.
It doesn't happen when a church leader falls into public immorality.
It doesn't happen when money disappears.
It doesn't happen when a ministry collapses.
This scandal often remains hidden beneath sermons, worship songs, ministry success, conference invitations, social media engagement, and crowded sanctuaries.
It hides behind smiles.
It disguises itself as passion.
It dresses itself as ministry.
And sometimes, the most dangerous idol in a church leader's life is not money, sex, power, or influence.
It is attention.
The kind of attention that slowly becomes more precious than obedience.
The kind of attention that quietly replaces intimacy with God.
The kind of attention that makes a person crave being seen more than being faithful.
Maybe that's why this story hurts.
Because it isn't only about church leaders.
It's about all of us.
Every one of us knows what it feels like to want approval.
To want recognition.
To want someone to notice us.
To want our efforts acknowledged.
To want our sacrifices appreciated.
To want our names remembered.
The human heart has always wrestled with this temptation.
Jesus exposed it openly.
In Matthew 6:1 He warned:
"Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them."
The Greek phrase "πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς" (pros to theathēnai autois) literally carries the idea of performing for observation, doing something specifically to attract attention.
Not serving.
Performing.
Not worshiping.
Displaying.
Not glorifying God.
Glorifying self.
The tragedy is that attention can feel so much like purpose that many never realize the difference.
A church leader stands before people.
The congregation listens.
Lives are touched.
Ministry grows.
Comments increase.
Followers multiply.
Invitations arrive.
The applause becomes louder.
The platform becomes larger.
And little by little, a subtle question emerges inside the soul:
"Am I still doing this for Jesus?"
Or...
"Am I doing this because I need them to need me?"
That question is terrifying because the heart is capable of incredible self-deception.
The prophet Jeremiah wrote:
"The heart is deceitful above all things."
Not some things.
Above all things.
The danger isn't merely that attention feels good.
The danger is that attention can become a counterfeit savior.
When affirmation becomes our oxygen, criticism feels like death.
When applause becomes our identity, silence feels unbearable.
When recognition becomes our reward, we stop seeking the reward of God.
Jesus confronted religious leaders who had mastered appearances while starving spiritually.
In John 5:44, He asked:
"How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
The word translated "glory" is the Greek word "δόξα" (doxa).
It carries the idea of honor, reputation, praise, recognition.
Jesus was exposing a devastating truth.
You cannot simultaneously chase the praise of people and the praise of God as your ultimate pursuit.
One will eventually dominate the other.
The scandal of attention is not that people admire you.
The scandal is when you begin needing it.
That is where many stories begin to unravel.
Yet Scripture is filled with people who discovered something even more powerful than attention.
Grace.
Because the Bible is not ultimately a collection of success stories.
It is a collection of rescue stories.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses murdered.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
The Gospel itself advances through broken people whose scandals were rewritten by grace.
That is why Christianity is unlike every man-made religion.
The foundation of our faith is not human perfection.
It is divine redemption.
At the center of everything stands Jesus Christ.
The One who possessed all glory yet humbled Himself.
Philippians 2 tells us that Christ "emptied Himself."
The Greek phrase is "ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν" (heauton ekenōsen).
The King of Heaven voluntarily laid aside privilege and embraced servanthood.
Imagine that.
The One most worthy of attention spent His earthly ministry redirecting attention to the Father.
The One deserving every crown chose a cross.
The One worthy of endless applause accepted mockery, rejection, betrayal, and humiliation.
Why?
Because love was greater than recognition.
Obedience was greater than popularity.
Redemption was greater than reputation.
And on that cross, Jesus absorbed every scandal.
The scandal of pride.
The scandal of hypocrisy.
The scandal of self-glory.
The scandal of our wandering hearts.
The Hebrew prophet Isaiah declared:
"All we like sheep have gone astray."
Not some.
All.
Every human heart has chased something other than God.
Every human heart has desired its own glory.
Every human heart has sought validation in places where only Christ can satisfy.
Yet the Gospel announces something breathtaking.
Grace is greater.
The New Testament word for grace is "χάρις" (charis).
It means unearned favor.
Unmerited kindness.
A gift that cannot be purchased.
A mercy that cannot be deserved.
A love that cannot be earned.
This is where the story changes.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
This is where Jesus rewrites everything.
The church leader who loved attention can repent.
The believer who secretly craves approval can repent.
The Christian who built identity around recognition can repent.
The exhausted soul trapped in performance can repent.
Because the Gospel is not an invitation to try harder.
It is an invitation to come home.
Come home to the Savior who already knows every hidden motive.
Come home to the Shepherd who sees beneath every mask.
Come home to the King who offers forgiveness instead of condemnation.
Perhaps while reading this, the Holy Spirit has gently exposed something hidden.
Not to shame you.
But to free you.
Not to condemn you.
But to restore you.
Maybe you've been serving while secretly starving.
Maybe you've been performing while quietly breaking.
Maybe you've been leading others while losing yourself.
Jesus is still calling.
Jesus is still healing.
Jesus is still restoring.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories.
If this message stirred something deep within you, don't keep it to yourself.
What part of this message challenged you most?
Your testimony may become someone else's turning point.
More than supporting content, you help expand a mission dedicated to biblical truth, discipleship, evangelism, encouragement, and reaching souls with the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
The applause fades.
The crowds leave.
The comments stop.
The platform eventually disappears.
But the soul that belongs to Jesus remains forever.
And when history closes and eternity opens, the greatest words we will ever hear will not come from a crowd.
They will come from Christ.
And in that moment, nothing else will matter.
The attention we chased will be forgotten.
The glory we accumulated will vanish.
Only Jesus will remain.
And somehow, beautifully, mercifully, eternally...
the Author of Grace will still be rewriting stories.
The greatest tragedy is not being forgotten by people—it is forgetting that Christ was always enough.
